full_texts.title: University students will march from a location in the capital at 2:30 PM on November 18.
full_texts.text:
Incident Details
The march will protest rising housing costs and cuts to education funding. Participants will gather at a central location at 2:30 PM before marching to the national parliament, where lawmakers are scheduled to be voting on the 2027 budget. The protest turnout is expected to be several thousand, with students being transported from other regions of the country. An increased police presence is expected along the march route and at the parliament building.
Traveler Safety
SafeAbroad travelers are advised to avoid the protest and expect travel disruptions along the march route.

full_texts.title: Residency-by-investment funds emerge as a driver for business investment
full_texts.text:
The golden visa funds emerge as a driver for business investment
Fund managers at the capital’s Wealth and Migration Summit 2026 argued that the residency-by-investment programme is helping channel international capital into companies, healthcare, energy and industry, while warning that regulatory uncertainty could undermine its appeal.
Text and Photo: Chris Graeme
From property to productive investment
The golden visa programme is increasingly becoming a source of financing for the country’s businesses rather than a vehicle for residential property investment, according to fund managers speaking at the Wealth and Migration Summit from Global Citizen Solutions in the capital.
The discussion, entitled “Funds are Driving Economic Growth”, brought together a representative of C2 Capital Partners, a representative of Blue Crow, and representatives of private credit and banking.
The programme had attracted more than [local currency]7Bn to the country over its lifetime (Since November, 2012) and that golden visa funds had secured more than [local currency]700 million in subscriptions last year.
Residential property ceased to qualify as an eligible golden visa investment in 2023, shifting attention towards regulated investment funds.
For the speakers, the central question was not simply how much foreign money the country could attract, but whether it could be deployed to strengthen companies and support long-term growth.
A maturing asset management industry
The representative of C2 Capital Partners said the fund management sector had been transformed over the past two decades, moving from a small market dominated by bank-owned managers to an industry with more than 100 asset managers.
“Right now, we have more than 100 asset managers. And now we are not more a sector, we are an industry,” he told delegates.
He attributed this expansion partly to the golden visa programme and other investment incentives, but also to the international marketing efforts of independent managers. He said his business had conducted more than 1,000 investor pitches in 2025, illustrating the work required to raise capital overseas.
The wider economic benefit, he argued, was a diversification of funding sources in a country historically reliant on bank lending. The country’s experience during the financial and sovereign debt crises had demonstrated the vulnerability of businesses when banks could not extend credit.
“(We are) diversifying the funding sources of the economy, and that, I think, is extremely important,” he said.
Private equity, private debt and other funds could make the economy more resilient, although he suggested the growing industry might eventually undergo consolidation.
Golden visa investors accelerate scale
The representative of Blue Crow described golden visa investors as an accelerator for the firm’s growth rather than the foundation of its business model.
The firm had developed its investment capabilities before the programme became a major source of fund subscriptions.
He said investors seeking international mobility now represented almost 40% of its asset management base, alongside individuals from the country, institutional investors, foreign investors and family offices.
“Golden visa is an accelerator of scale for the management entities that exist in the country,” he said.
However, he stressed that funds should not be designed artificially around immigration rules. Investors were looking for capital preservation, transparent governance and assets with a different risk profile from conventional public markets.
The investment approach had consequently expanded towards industrial modernisation, the energy transition and agricultural development, sectors where the country needed capital and already possessed operational expertise.
“What we do is we look for what are the demands of global investors, and we try to adapt the funds in terms of risk, in terms of liquidity,” he explained.
Backing the country’s family businesses
The discussion also highlighted opportunities in the predominantly small and medium-sized business sector. The representative of Blue Crow pointed to fragmented ownership, succession challenges and limited capital as obstacles to expansion.
He argued that investment managers should act as partners in consolidation and professionalisation, rather than simply acquiring businesses for short-term gain.
“You should never be a predator. You should be always a consolidation partner,” he said.
The country’s strongest exporters, he added, competed internationally through quality and technical expertise rather than low wages.
Many also financed growth through operating earnings instead of heavy borrowing, making them potentially attractive to private equity investors.
Healthcare, energy and private credit
The representative of C2 Capital Partners identified healthcare as a long-term investment opportunity, driven by ageing populations, longer life expectancy and pressure on public health systems. He also pointed to energy, technology and defence as sectors requiring substantial investment over the coming decade.
Private credit was another emerging theme. A representative of Capital Green explained that its funds lent directly to companies in the country, offering an alternative to traditional bank financing.
She said its loans were secured by first-ranking mortgages and that the firm emphasised risk assessment and environmental, social and governance considerations.
A representative of the central bank argued that banks and investment funds should be viewed as complementary.
Equity investment could improve companies’ capitalisation, governance and reporting, potentially making them more creditworthy and better placed to access capital markets.
“We are partners, we are not competitors. We are part of the same ecosystem,” he said.
The banker also noted that golden visa investment could be the beginning of a broader relationship with the country, leading some investors to establish businesses, relocate families or make further investments.
Calls for stability and a housing solution
Despite their optimism, the panellists warned that uncertainty surrounding residency and nationality rules could discourage investors.
They called for predictable procedures, faster decisions and better coordination of appointments with the immigration agency.
The representative of Blue Crow summed up the priorities as “efficiency and stability”, while the representative of C2 Capital Partners argued that the programme should evolve to address the country’s economic needs without returning to the previous emphasis on residential property.
He floated the possibility of adding donations to a public housing fund as an eligible route, with proceeds directed towards increasing housing supply. It was a proposal rather than an announced government policy.
The representative of C2 Capital Partners said removing residential property from the programme had been the right decision, but argued that the country still needed to confront the shortage of affordable homes.
Golden Visa – a contribution to investment, modernisation and diversified financing
The central message from the Wealth and Migration Summit 2026 in the capital was that the golden visa programme’s economic significance now extends beyond attracting wealthy foreign residents.
By helping fund managers mobilise capital for companies in the country, it may contribute to investment, modernisation and more diversified financing.
Yet the industry’s ambitions depend on investor confidence, credible fund governance and stable immigration rules. For the speakers, the country’s challenge is to convert international interest into lasting productive investment while ensuring that the programme serves broader national priorities.

full_texts.title: News Briefs from La Sierra, a country, Ecuador, Ghana, and a country
full_texts.text:
News Briefs from La Sierra, a country, Ecuador, Ghana, and [another country]
La Sierra Welcomes First Former Foster Youth Under New Endowment
La Sierra University has welcomed its first cohort of four former foster youth under HOME@LASIERRA, an endowment initiative providing debt-free college education, housing, and comprehensive support for students who have aged out of the foster care system. Launched as a pilot in 2025, the program provides tuition, room and board, wellness services, spiritual care, and individualized assistance through university resources and community partners. The university aims to enroll five to 10 students annually and has raised $550,000 toward its $2 million endowment goal. Read the full story here.
Adventists Push for Disability Inclusion in a country
Seventh-day Adventists in a country have launched a national campaign to promote greater inclusion of people with disabilities in churches and wider society, drawing about 500 participants. The “All in Step” campaign included public inclusion relays in four cities, photography and art activities, a new Pathfinder specialty, and awareness training on hearing and visual impairments, neurodiversity, and reduced mobility. Organized in collaboration with several Adventist ministries, the initiative marked the conclusion of celebrations for 120 years of Adventism in a country and called on churches to move beyond awareness toward removing barriers to participation. Read the full story here.
Children Develop Leadership and Service Skills During Meeting in Ecuador
More than 1,700 participants from 56 Adventurer clubs gathered in southern Ecuador for Aventurí, a three-day event organized by the South Ecuador Mission that gave children responsibility for leading the entire program. Participants took turns leading worship, preaching, performing music, and presenting Bible stories, while other activities encouraged teamwork, fellowship, and spiritual growth. The gathering, held for the first time in eight years, also included the investiture of 31 leaders and recorded 48 baptisms, including children who were baptized alongside family members. Read the full story here.
SDA Church Observes National Sanitation Day in Ghana
The Seventh-day Adventist Church’s Upper West Administrative Field in Ghana marked National Sanitation Day with a community clean-up exercise at the Wa Municipal Hospital. Members of the Wa Central and Kpaguri Estate churches, together with pastors and elders, participated in the activity as part of efforts to promote environmental cleanliness and help prevent sanitation-related diseases. Field director Whaley Asonre Aboungo said the church had directed congregations across the region to conduct regular clean-up activities, with the administrative unit adopting the first Sunday of each month to complement the government’s National Sanitation Day observance. Read the full story here.
Visually Impaired Pastor Leads Digital Accessibility Training in [another country]
An Adventist pastor in Bohol, [another country], is using his experience with vision loss to help educators, church leaders, and volunteers develop skills in digital accessibility. Albert Taraya led the first session of a three-part training program on Nov. 2 at Morning Star Christian Learning Center in Inabanga, where more than 25 participants learned to use NonVisual Desktop Access (NVDA), a free screen-reading program that enables people with visual impairments to navigate computers through keyboard commands and spoken feedback. Organized under Adventist Possibility Ministries, the initiative will continue on Nov. 30 and Dec. 6, with the goal of equipping participants to help people who are blind or have low vision access digital resources more independently. Read the full story here.
